description:
Tung Tung Tung Sahur Squad is our team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Together, we created Flame in Freefall, an interactive project that makes NASA’s microgravity fire research easier to explore and understand.
Our team consists of Hafizov Yusuf, and Muhammad Parvizzoda. Yusuf was responsible for the user interface and 3D models, shaping how visitors experience the virtual Fire Lab. Muhammad handled backend and code development, building the systems that power the project.
summary:
Fire Lab is an interactive web platform that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into accessible fire-safety insights. We developed a 3D spacecraft laboratory where users explore how gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and fuel affect flame behaviour, then compare those conditions with real NASA experiments.

Addressing the **Flame in Freefall** challenge, Fire Lab brings together research from investigations such as BASS, FLEX, and SAFFIRE. Users can compare experiments, explore data gaps, export datasets, and ask an AI analyst questions supported by NASA sources. Visualizations distinguish illustrative flame behavior from measured results and clearly identify conditions where evidence is missing.

Fire safety becomes increasingly important as people travel farther from Earth and spend longer in spacecraft and planetary habitats. Fire Lab helps students, researchers, and mission planners understand the available evidence, recognize its limitations, and identify questions that future experiments must answer to better protect crews.
details:
Fire Lab is an interactive web platform that helps people explore NASA’s combustion research and understand what it tells us about fire safety in space. We developed it for the Flame in Freefall challenge to make complex experimental data easier to find, compare, interpret, and use. The platform combines a 3D spacecraft laboratory, searchable experiment records, data visualizations, comparison tools, and an AI analyst.

The project begins with a practical problem: fire does not behave the same way in microgravity as it does on Earth. Changes in gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and fuel can affect combustion. Understanding those differences matters for crewed spacecraft, space stations, and future habitats on the Moon and Mars. However, the evidence is spread across experimental tables, research papers, and investigation records. Fire Lab brings these resources into a shared interface and connects explanations to their sources.

Users enter a virtual spacecraft laboratory containing a flame chamber, control console, and data monitors. They can adjust gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and material, or select a preset representing a mission environment. The flame responds visually, helping users explore the physical relationships behind combustion. The visualization is clearly identified as an illustrative model, rather than a complete simulation of a real spacecraft fire.

The laboratory connects these settings to experimental evidence. A coverage indicator compares the selected conditions with ranges represented in the project’s NASA datasets. Users can see whether their configuration falls within those ranges or extends beyond them. The interface also retrieves nearby experimental conditions, allowing users to inspect the material, atmosphere, airflow, crew observations, and original source record. A nearby experiment is presented as a comparison, not proof that the selected configuration is safe.

For fuel droplets, the project includes a more specific mathematical model based on the d² law, which describes the reduction of a burning droplet’s squared diameter over time. Burning-rate estimates are fitted to FLEX experimental data, while related test outcomes help illustrate where burning ends. This gives users an example of how an experimental dataset can support a model, while making the model’s assumptions and limitations visible.

Beyond the laboratory, Fire Lab provides tools for examining the research itself. Users can explore investigations such as BASS, FLEX, SAFFIRE, ACME, and SAME, compare their objectives and experimental conditions, and examine their relevance to different fire-safety questions. An adjustable ranking system helps organize investigations by criteria such as material flammability, detection, suppression, and mission relevance. Its scoring is identified as a project-defined interpretation, not an official NASA safety rating.

The platform also highlights gaps in the available evidence. This is especially important when considering partial gravity or atmospheric conditions proposed for future habitats. Instead of filling those gaps with invented measurements, Fire Lab shows where relevant data are missing. Users can export structured data in CSV or JSON formats, with source information and field descriptions, to support further analysis.

The AI analyst provides another way to explore the material. Users can enter a short keyword, such as “Mars,” “smoke,” or “FLEX,” or ask a more detailed question. Our OpenAI integration uses GPT-4.1 mini to explain relevant NASA records and provide source links. Responses can include NASA imagery and charts calculated from the project’s datasets. The charts use recorded values and explicit calculations rather than numbers generated by the language model. The API key remains on the server and is excluded from the public website and source-control history.

We used the following technologies to develop the project:

  • HTML and CSS for the interface, responsive layouts, controls, and presentation styling.
  • JavaScript, Three.js, and WebGL for the interactive spacecraft environment, flame visualization, camera movement, and browser-based tools.
  • Python for data preparation, validation, packaging, and the local AI service.
  • NASA PSI datasets and NASA NTRS research resources as the scientific foundation for the platform.
  • The OpenAI Responses API for the connected AI analyst.
  • Git and GitHub for collaboration, version control, and feature development.
  • Automated Python and JavaScript checks for data calculations, interface logic, source handling, and packaging.

The project runs on ordinary computers and compatible mobile browsers; it does not require custom hardware or physical combustion equipment. Graphics settings help accommodate devices with different capabilities. English and Russian interfaces, guided explanations, and a separate presentation website make the work accessible to a wider audience.

The project’s creative approach is to place scientific evidence inside an interactive environment. Users can change a condition, observe an illustrative response, and immediately investigate the supporting data. The spacecraft monitors become tools for understanding experimental coverage, while the console encourages exploration. This connects the visual experience to scientific questions rather than treating the 3D scene as decoration.

Throughout development, our team considered scientific accuracy, traceability, usability, performance, and responsible use of AI. We distinguished measured results from model outputs and assumptions, preserved links to source records, and avoided presenting missing data as established knowledge. We also considered differences between experiment types: results from a burning liquid droplet, for example, cannot automatically establish the safety of a solid cabin material.

Our intended impact is to make NASA’s research more useful to students, educators, researchers, and people exploring future mission requirements. Fire Lab supports learning, evidence discovery, and the identification of unanswered questions. By helping users understand both what the data show and what they cannot establish, the project encourages better-informed research and discussion about protecting future crews.
dataRefs: PSI Data Repository: Combustion Science: Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) source of the data upon which the NASA Space App is to be based.
NASA Combustion Science: Basic information about most of the combustion investigations for which data is found in the PSI Data Repository.
NASA ScienceCasts: The Power of Studying Combustion on the ISS: Introduction to NASA’s combustion research on the International Space Station through a 3.6-minute video clip from 2018.

A Researcher’s Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science: A 2015 review of NASA’s combustion research conducted on, or planned for, the International Space Station. Basic information about most of the combustion investigations described in this 50+ page document is found within the PSI Data Repository.
Apollo 1: Information about the crew mission, fire that erupted during a pre-launch test killing the crew, investigation, and lessons learned.
Apollo 13: Information about the crew, mission, oxygen tank explosion that occurred during the flight to the Moon, investigation, and lessons learned.

25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Basic information about a fire—caused by an oxygen generator failure—that erupted within the Russian space station Mir in 1997 during joint operations in preparation for the International Space Station (first occupied in 2000).
Fireman’s Air Tanks: Basic information about the 1970s adaptation of spacesuit technology to improve firefighters’ air tanks and breathing gear.

Fire Detector: Basic information about a 1970s smoke detector developed for the shuttle that, discriminating between smoke and dust, results in less nuisance alarms. As such, it has industrial applications (e.g., in mining operations).
New Technology for the Fire Attire: Basic information about a 1980s application of NASA spacesuit technology to improve firefighter clothing.
Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes
Correlation of Normal Gravity Mixed Convection Blowoff Limits with Microgravity Forced Flow Blowoff Limits
